reason: Heating rocky planetesimals should start forming the differentiated interiors needed to expose stone and metal.
expectation: I expect internal radioactive heating to produce a warmer or melted rocky body, though further steps may be needed to separate its materials.

alternatives.reason: Heating icy bodies may advance the water-in-rock goal, but I chose to follow the rocky route first.

effect: The rocky body has melted, so gravity may now separate its materials.
reaction: The qualification that not all asteroids melt is a useful detail.
reason: Gravity can separate denser metal from lighter rock in the melted body.
expectation: I expect a differentiated body with a metal-rich interior and rocky outer layers.

alternatives.reason: Heating the icy bodies would advance the other goal, but I want to continue the rocky route first.

effect: The metal has separated into a core, making the body ready to be broken apart.
reaction: It's satisfying to see differentiation occur before Earth forms.
reason: Collisions seem the direct way to expose stone and metal from the differentiated body.
expectation: I expect the collision to break the small world and expose material from its rocky layers and metal core.

alternatives.reason: Cooling might solidify the body first, but collisions more directly match the goal.

effect: The collision exposed core metal; cooling the differentiated body may help reveal the remaining stone.
reaction: The connection to iron meteorites is a useful detail.
reason: I'll cool the differentiated body to continue the stone-and-metal goal.
expectation: I expect the body to solidify, potentially enabling rocky fragments to be exposed later.

alternatives.reason: Heating icy planetesimals could advance the water goal, but I want to continue the rocky route.

effect: The asteroid's outer rock has solidified, so a collision may expose rocky fragments.
reaction: The cooling step makes the rocky exterior's formation clear.
reason: A collision should break the cooled asteroid and advance the stone-and-metal goal.
expectation: I expect fragments of its solid rocky exterior, possibly alongside metal.

alternatives.reason: Heating icy planetesimals would advance the other goal, but I want to finish the rocky route first.

effect: The rocky fragments complete the first goal; I can now follow the icy-body route.
reaction: The contrast between core metal and rocky layers is clear.
reason: Heating icy planetesimals is the only offered combination and should advance the water-in-rock goal.
expectation: I expect internal heating to melt some ice, potentially allowing water to react with rock.

effect: Internal heating produced confined liquid water, ready to react with silicate rock.
reaction: The possibility of liquid water beneath a frozen exterior is intriguing.
reason: The only offered combination should advance the goal of retaining water in altered rock.
expectation: I expect water to react with the silicates and form water-bearing altered minerals.

effect: The water–silicate reaction completed the final goal and showed how hydrated rock can carry hydrogen even after exposed ice is gone.
reaction: That link between hidden water reactions and Earth's volatile ingredients was intriguing.

mostWorthwhile.text: Reacting liquid water with silicates was most worthwhile: it connected an icy body's interior to water-bearing rock and Earth's ingredients.

leastWorthwhile.text: The separate cooling and second collision on the rocky route felt somewhat repetitive, although they clarified how solid rocky fragments arise.

surprise.text: I was surprised that a frozen-looking body could conceal liquid water and water–rock reactions.

arbitrary.text: The need for a separate collision after cooling was not obvious at first, though the result explained the distinction between exposed core metal and solid rocky layers.

continue.text: Yes. The connections between asteroid interiors, meteorites and water-bearing minerals make me curious how those ingredients contribute to the growing Earth.
